body.heading: What counts as sand
paragraphs: To a geologist, sand is a size, not a substance: grains between about 0.06 and 2 millimetres across. Smaller is silt, larger is gravel. Most beach and desert sand is quartz, simply because quartz is hard, common and stubborn — it survives journeys that grind softer minerals to dust.

But sand can be almost anything small and durable. Tropical white beaches are often ground-up coral and shell. Hawaiian black sand is shattered volcanic glass and lava. There are green sands of olivine and pink sands tinted by garnet.

body.heading: Reading a handful
paragraphs: The grains tell their own travel story. Rounded, frosted grains suggest long tumbling by wind in a desert. Sharp, angular grains are freshly broken, close to their source rock. Geologists read sand the way you might read a postmark.

Sand is also surprisingly precious. It is the raw material of concrete, glass and computer chips, and the world uses it in staggering quantities — tens of billions of tonnes a year. The humblest handful on the beach is part of one of Earth's great recycling systems.

takeaway: Sand is defined by grain size, and each handful records a journey of breaking, travelling and sorting.
